_**Agent (default)**_

Decart’s realtime docs recommend a different kind of reference for each mode in this studio. Use JPEG, PNG, or WebP, at least 512×512, under about 5 MB, and under 2048 px on the longest side so uploads stay fast.

**Character** (`lucy-latest`)

Use a clear, front-facing head-and-shoulders portrait. Even lighting, a neutral background, a centered face, and a neutral or mild expression transfer best. Higher resolution keeps more identity detail.

Avoid a covered face, profile or tilted shots, blur, more than one face, and any image that is not a face.

**Restyle** (`lucy-restyle-2`)

Use artwork or an illustration with a strong look: a distinct palette, texture, and lighting, in a simple composition. Paintings and digital art transfer better than photos.

Avoid ordinary photos of real scenes, very dark or blown-out images, and images with a lot of text.

**Try-on** (`lucy-vton-latest`)

Use the garment alone on a white or plain background, with no person in the frame. The model copies what it sees, so the item should be sharp and complete. If the source is a model wearing the clothes, extract just the garment onto white first and keep its real color, shape, and details.

Sources: [Reference Images](https://docs.platform.decart.ai/models/realtime/reference-images), [Virtual Try-On](https://docs.platform.decart.ai/models/realtime/virtual-try-on), [VTON prompting](https://docs.platform.decart.ai/models/realtime/vton-3.5-prompting).

_**Agent (default)**_

A full-body photo and a background or style change are two different jobs. Decart wants a different image for each.

**Full-body character or outfit**

On Lucy 2.5, match the reference to the camera. If the live shot shows a standing person from head to feet, use a full-body reference with the whole person visible and centered, on a plain background. A head-and-shoulders crop is the wrong reference for that shot.

On the older character model, a full-body photo is weaker because the face gets too small. That model still prefers a sharp, front-facing head-and-shoulders portrait.

For clothes only, keep using Try-on: the garment alone on white, with no person in the picture.

**Changing the background**

Use a photo of the place, and keep the prompt only about the place:

`Change the background to a Mediterranean street with flags blowing in the breeze.`

The image is a look guide. Lucy fits it to your camera angle, so it will not copy the layout exactly. A clean, well-lit camera background helps. Describe motion in the new scene, such as water, flags, or lights, and match the light direction and time of day to the person. Extra instructions about the person in that same prompt tend to change the person too.

**Changing the whole style**

That is Restyle, not a background swap. Use a painting or illustration with a clear palette, texture, and lighting. A normal photo of a room or street is a weak style reference. One style per prompt works best, for example “Transform the entire scene into a watercolor painting with translucent washes and paper texture.”

Sources: [Lucy 2.5](https://docs.platform.decart.ai/models/realtime/lucy-2.5), [Lucy 2.5 prompting](https://docs.platform.decart.ai/models/realtime/lucy-2.5-prompting), [Reference images](https://docs.platform.decart.ai/models/realtime/reference-images).

Pasting a screenshot anywhere on the studio page should set the reference image. The dropzone will handle paste events while focused. A document-level paste listener will also catch pasted images when no text input is active.

The window paste listener will apply the image only when the dropzone is focused or the paste target is inside it. It will also trigger if no editable field is active and the dropzone is empty. This catches Ctrl+V without requiring a click.

Image validation logic will be extracted into a reusable helper for both the dropzone and document listeners. The document-level paste handler will skip targets that are inputs, textareas, or contenteditable elements to avoid intercepting normal text pastes. Since the user specifically highlighted the empty dropzone, the paste feature will be limited to that state.

Paste will be wired exclusively to the empty dropzone. Replacing an existing reference image is out of scope; users can use Replace for that.

Pasting will also replace an existing reference image, not just the empty dropzone. The document-level paste listener will catch Ctrl+V even when the body is focused, such as after copying from another application. A reusable `acceptReferenceFile` helper is being drafted to validate image files against MIME types and the 10 MB size limit.

Implementing a clipboard paste handler for the dropzone.

Refining the paste listener scope. It will trigger only when the dropzone is focused or the paste target is inside it. This prevents clipboard images from entering editable fields.

Adding a "or paste" hint to the dropzone. A document-level listener will route image pastes to the dropzone when no text field is focused. This matches the expected reference image picker behavior. Constants for the 10 MB limit and accepted image MIME types are being defined.

Writing the `imageFileFromClipboard` helper to extract image files from DataTransfer objects. Starting the `isTextEntry` utility to detect editable input fields.

An `acceptReference` callback was added to handle accepted files. It validates size and MIME type, revokes the previous object URL, creates a new one, updates state, and clears errors.

The `onDrop` handler is being refactored to call `acceptReference`. The paste effect will skip editable targets and extract image files from clipboard data.

The paste effect will prevent default browser behavior and invoke `acceptReference` when an image is found. It will skip pastes once a reference image is already set. An explicit `onPaste` handler will also be attached directly to the Dropzone element.

The user wants to know if their phone can act as a web recorder while still working with OBS, without changing any code.

No code changes are needed. One approach uses the phone browser as the studio source while OBS runs on the PC. This only works if the phone opens a reachable URL, that origin is allowed, and the connection is secure. Localhost or LAN HTTP is not a secure context, so the phone camera will be blocked unless HTTPS or a tunnel is used.

The phone browser must stay open and active. The browser that starts the live stream owns the camera. OBS on the PC only watches the AI output page. The phone camera feeds the studio directly.

A simpler workaround avoids the secure-context problem entirely. Keep the studio open on the PC. Run a local webcam app on the phone such as Iriun, DroidCam, Camo, or iPhone Continuity Camera. Select that virtual camera in the PC dropdown and start the stream. OBS does not need any changes.

_**Agent (default)**_

Yes. The phone can be the camera, and OBS can still show the AI video. They are two separate jobs.

The browser where you press **Start live** is the only camera. OBS does not see the phone. It only opens the `/obs` page and shows the transformed video after that session starts.

**Phone as the camera in this site**

Open the studio in the phone browser, allow the camera, and press **Start live**. Leave that page open. On the computer, keep the OBS Browser Source on the `/obs` link.

`http://localhost:3000` on the phone is the phone itself, so it cannot reach the studio running on the computer. The phone needs the computer’s real address, and that exact address has to be in `APP_ORIGINS`. The phone browser will also refuse the camera on a plain `http://192.168…` address. It needs `localhost` or HTTPS.

The phone tab has to stay awake and in the foreground. If the screen locks or the browser pauses the page, the camera and the OBS picture stop.

**Easier setup with this app as it is**

Keep the studio and OBS on the computer. Use the phone as a webcam the computer browser can select, with an app such as Camo, Iriun, DroidCam, or iPhone Continuity Camera. Choose that camera in the studio dropdown, then press **Start live**. OBS stays on the same Browser Source.
